echo accepts multiple comma-separated arguments and prints them in order.
print is a language construct that always returns 1, so it can be used within expressions.
The elvis operator `$a ?: $b` returns its left operand when it is truthy, and the right operand when it is falsy.
PHP 8 moved the concatenation operator's precedence below arithmetic operators like + and -, so '1 . 2 + 3' evaluates as 1 . (2+3).
The ** operator is right-associative in PHP, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 equals 2 ** 9 = 512.
In PHP 8, '+' has higher precedence than '.', so ('sum: ' . 2) + 3 is evaluated as the string 'sum: 2' cast to number 0, plus 3 = 3.
With ===, arrays must have the same key/value pairs in the same order and of the same types.
0 == false is a loose comparison and evaluates to true; strict comparison would use ===.
Since PHP 8, comparing a non-numeric string to a number converts the number to a string, so "abc" == 0 is false.

In loose comparison, null == 0, null == "", and null == false are all true (in PHP versions before 8.0's stricter string comparisons, and null still loosely equals "" and false in 8+; null == 0 is also still true since 0 is not a numeric string).
Casting a string to int takes the leading numeric portion, so '42abc' becomes 42.
PHP coerces the numeric string '5' to an integer, so addition yields 10.
false cast to string yields an empty string "", while true yields "1".
Due to floating-point precision, 0.1+0.2 equals 0.30000000000000004, which is not identical to 0.3.
strrev() reverses bytes, which corrupts multi-byte UTF-8 characters.
str_contains returns true because the substring 'world' exists in 'Hello world'.
str_pad() can pad on the right (default), left, or both sides using the optional pad_type argument.
By default trim() strips whitespace characters including spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns, null bytes, and vertical tabs.
strlen counts bytes, and 'é' is encoded as 2 bytes in UTF-8, so 5 characters become 6 bytes.
A negative start of -3 counts from the end of the string, returning the last 3 characters 'def'.
Strings are immutable in PHP; ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character uppercased.
Heredoc interpolates variables like double-quoted strings, while nowdoc treats text literally like single-quoted strings.
sort() reindexes the array with numeric keys, so it does not preserve key-to-value associations (unlike asort()).
PHP casts numeric string keys like '5' to integers automatically when used as array keys.
in_array() uses loose comparison (==) by default; strict comparison requires passing true as the third parameter.
When called without a callback, array_filter() removes all elements that evaluate to false (e.g., 0, "", null, [], false).
By default array_slice() reindexes numeric keys; you must pass true as the preserve_keys parameter to keep them.
array_slice extracts 2 elements starting at offset 1, returning [20, 30].
The + union keeps all keys, with left-side values winning on duplicates, so the array is ['a'=>1,'b'=>2].
Since PHP 8.1, array unpacking with the spread operator supports string keys, e.g. [...$a, ...$b] where the arrays have string keys.
Named arguments can be combined with argument unpacking, as unpacked arrays may contain string keys treated as named arguments (PHP 8.1+).
Anonymous functions in PHP do not automatically inherit outer scope variables; they must be explicitly imported with the use clause (or arrow functions).
func_num_args() returns the actual number of arguments passed to the function, not the declared parameters.
Arrow functions can have a body wrapped in curly braces containing multiple statements, though then a return statement is needed.
Arrow functions capture outer variables by value automatically, and by-reference capture is not possible.
A static closure cannot automatically bind $this, so it does not capture the current object context.
Closures capture variables by value at creation time, so the later change to $x does not affect it.
In weak mode, numeric strings like "5" are coerced to int.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0.
The final keyword prevents a method from being overridden in subclasses.
A final method cannot be overridden by child classes.
Private properties of a parent class are not accessible in a subclass; only public and protected members are.
An anonymous class gets a generated name of the form 'class@anonymous' + NUL + file path + line, so the part before the NUL byte is 'class@anonymous'.
Private methods are not inherited or overridable, so a child class can freely redeclare a method with the same name and any visibility.
__get() is called for inaccessible properties, including private/protected ones, not only non-existent ones.
Reassigning a readonly property throws an Error (specifically it triggers an Error exception, not Exception).
PHP interfaces can declare constants, which are inherited by implementing classes.
The instanceof operator checks whether an object is an instance of a class or implements an interface.
Since PHP 5.3, interfaces may declare static methods that implementing classes must define.
instanceof checks both class inheritance and interface implementations.
PHP interface methods may only declare a signature and cannot contain a body or default implementation, unlike trait methods.
Abstract methods may be public, protected, or (in PHP 7.1+) private-adjacent rules aside, protected is allowed; only visibility must match or be weaker in child implementations.
cases() returns an array of all enum cases, and Foo defines three cases: A, B, and C.
Since PHP 8.2, traits can declare constants, which become class constants in the classes that use the trait.
In PHP 7+, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface.
TypeError extends Error, not Exception, so a catch (Exception) block will not catch it.
The @ operator only suppresses errors and warnings raised by expressions, not exceptions, which still propagate.
intdiv() with a zero divisor throws DivisionByZeroError.
The finally block runs regardless of whether an exception was thrown or caught.
An exception thrown in a finally block propagates and overrides any pending return value or exception from the try block.
Casting an object (like an Exception instance) to bool always yields true.
Shutdown functions run after script execution ends, including when exit() or die() is called.
The use statement only creates an alias; the class file is loaded when the class is actually used (e.g., instantiated), typically via autoloading.
In PHP namespace imports, `use function` imports functions while `use const` imports constants.
The App\ prefix is stripped and the remaining namespace maps to directories under src/.
Composer's generated autoloader uses spl_autoload_register() to register its class-loading functions.
The __NAMESPACE__ magic constant holds the name of the current namespace.

An unqualified class name is resolved relative to the current namespace (with fallback for namespaced code only in some cases), not from the global root — only fully qualified names with a leading \ refer to the global root.
PSR-4 replaces the namespace prefix App\ with src/, so App\Model\User maps to src/Model/User.php.
Use statements are compile-time aliases with file (or namespace block) scope, not function scope, so placing one inside a function still affects the entire file from that point on.
In PHP, arrays are value types, so assignment copies the array unless you explicitly reference it with &.
$b is a copy of $a, so appending to $b doesn't affect $a.
Inside a function only local variables are visible unless you import them via the global keyword, the $GLOBALS array, or parameters.
unset($GLOBALS['x']) actually removes the global variable completely, since $GLOBALS directly accesses the global scope.
The parameter is passed by reference, so incrementing $x modifies $n.
When iterating by value, foreach operates on a copy of the array, so modifications inside the loop do not affect the iteration.
A static property belongs to the class itself, shared across all instances, so changes are visible to all objects.
PHP casts boolean array keys to integers: true becomes 1 and false becomes 0.
Since PHP 7, a generator can return a final value via return, retrieved with the getReturn() method once the generator finishes.

Calling a generator function returns an object of the built-in Generator class.

SplStack implements a LIFO stack; SplQueue is the FIFO queue.
ArrayIterator wraps an array so it can be traversed using the Iterator interface methods (rewind, current, key, next, valid).
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so it can be traversed with foreach.
Since PHP 5.5, password_hash() automatically generates a secure salt, and the salt option is deprecated.
PASSWORD_DEFAULT currently uses bcrypt (via password_hash), not md5.
password_verify correctly verifies the plaintext 'secret' against the freshly generated hash of the same string.
strip_tags() removes HTML tags and has nothing to do with SQL injection; use prepared statements for that.
Calling session_regenerate_id() after login replaces the session ID, preventing attackers from fixing a known session ID.
php_sapi_name() returns the current Server API name, such as 'cli'.
session_destroy() removes server-side session data; the client cookie must be cleared separately, e.g., with setcookie().
PHP only populates $_SESSION after session_start() is called (or session.auto_start is enabled).
array_find() was introduced in PHP 8.4.
Property hooks (get/set in property declarations) were introduced in PHP 8.4.
PHP 8.4 introduced asymmetric visibility with the syntax public private(set), allowing different read and write scopes.
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.5.
The pipe operator |> was introduced in PHP 8.5.
The clone($obj, ['prop' => value]) syntax (clone with arguments) was introduced in PHP 8.4.
array_first() and array_last() were introduced in PHP 8.5.
The Partial Function Application v2 RFC was accepted targeting PHP 8.5.
The clamp_v2 RFC was implemented in PHP 8.5, released late 2025.
The Context Managers RFC (introducing Python-like `using` blocks) has not been adopted into PHP as of November 2026.
The generics RFC has not been declined; it remains an open/draft proposal rather than being rejected in 2026.
No RFC has been accepted to make ZTS (multithreading) the default build of PHP; PHP remains NTS by default as of that date.
PHP 8.5 does not support generics; parameterized types remain unimplemented.

PHP 6 was abandoned and versioning jumped from PHP 5.6 to PHP 7.0.
The #[\Deprecated] attribute was added to PHP core in PHP 8.4 via an adopted RFC.
Clean and onion architectures require dependencies to point inward, with inner layers unaware of outer layers.
Domain entities should be plain PHP classes (with optional standard library usage) to remain framework-agnostic.
Controllers and templates belong to the presentation/interface layer, not the business-logic layer; use cases themselves form the business logic.
Onion architecture places the domain model (entities/core business logic) at the center, with layers like services and infrastructure surrounding it.
Tools like deptrac statically analyze class dependencies and fail the build when a layer calls a forbidden layer.
Use cases should operate on domain-level inputs and abstractions, not framework artifacts like HTTP requests or ORM EntityManagers, to remain decoupled from delivery and infrastructure layers.
In Domain-Driven Design, a Repository provides a collection-like interface over aggregates/entities while hiding the underlying storage.
In clean architecture, infrastructure details like the database are isolated in the outer layer behind interfaces, so swapping PostgreSQL doesn't affect the domain or use cases.
An aggregate is a domain-driven design concept: a cluster of domain objects treated as a single consistency unit with a root entity, not merely a database table.
A Value Object is defined by being immutable and equal based on its field values rather than object identity.
In Domain-Driven Design, the aggregate root is the only entry point through which external code may modify the aggregate.
Repositories provide a collection-like interface per aggregate root; inner entities are accessed only through the aggregate.
Ubiquitous language in Domain-Driven Design is the shared vocabulary used by developers and domain experts.
A model's vocabulary defines the set of tokens it understands consistently; outside it, tokens are split differently, so the same words can mean other things.
DDD recommends rich domain models that encapsulate behavior, not anemic models with logic pushed into services.
In domain-driven design, a bounded context defines a boundary within which a model is consistent, so the same real-world concept may be represented by different classes in different contexts.
Symfony services are instantiated lazily — only when first requested from the container.
Symfony's console command `php bin/console debug:router` lists all registered routes.
Symfony can autowire services automatically using autoconfigure and autowiring defaults, without manually declaring each one.
Twig compiles templates into PHP classes and caches them, so they are reused across requests.
In dev mode Symfony caches the compiled container and only rebuilds it when one of its tracked resources (config files, classes, etc.) changes.
Symfony reads the APP_ENV environment variable to determine the active environment (e.g., dev or prod).
Symfony controller actions must be public methods; routing cannot invoke private (or protected) methods.
Subscribers and listeners are dispatched in the same order determined by their priority and registration order, not by interface type.
Symfony 6.0 removed the guard authenticator system entirely, keeping only the authenticator-based security system.
Symfony's #[IsGranted('ROLE_...')] attribute denies access with a 403 if the role/voter fails.
Symfony voters are indeed the mechanism for granting or denying access to specific objects via isGranted()/authorizeAttrribute checks.
Symfony 7 removed doctrine/annotations support, so validation constraints must use PHP attributes like #[Assert\NotBlank].
Symfony forms include CSRF protection by default, and the token is automatically validated on submission.
Symfony form validation is always performed server-side on submission, regardless of client-side HTML5 validation results.
The Symfony maker bundle's `make:form` command generates a FormType class.
Symfony never stores the raw password in the session; it uses the encoded password (or token-based authentication) instead.
Symfony stores each bundle's configuration in a separate file under config/packages, typically named after the bundle or topic (e.g., framework.yaml, twig.yaml).
This is the standard Symfony practice: .env holds committed dev defaults while .env.local contains real, non-committed secrets.
The `debug:container` console command lists registered services and their aliases in the service container.
The Symfony container is frozen after compilation, so setParameter() cannot be used at runtime from a controller.
Since Symfony 3.4/4.0, services are private by default and can only be injected via dependency injection, not fetched directly from the container.
Bundles work with sensible defaults; a config file in config/packages is optional and only needed to override defaults.
Symfony's services.yaml uses %env(VAR)% to inject environment variable values.
Symfony uses the APP_DEBUG environment variable (typically set in .env) to enable or disable debug mode, including the profiler and Twig debugging.
A message can have multiple handlers in Symfony Messenger; when it does, it's handled by all of them (unless handled by a single handler via the HandleTrait approach).
The sync transport processes the message immediately in the same process instead of queueing it for a worker.
Symfony Messenger workers are started with the messenger:consume command (e.g. php bin/console messenger:consume async).
In Symfony Messenger, the retry_strategy (e.g. multiplier) can be configured individually for each transport under the transports configuration.
By default, Symfony Messenger serializes messages using PHP's native serialize() format (PhpSerializer), not JSON.
Symfony's Scheduler component schedules messages and sends them via Messenger transports to be consumed by workers.
The built-in Messenger transport named 'doctrine' stores queued messages in database tables managed via Doctrine.
Symfony Messenger allows adding custom middleware to the stack, configured before or after built-in middleware.
Symfony follows a fixed schedule with major releases every two years and six minor releases, including two standard releases each year in May and November.
Symfony 8 requires PHP 8.2 or higher.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for docblock annotations; only PHP attributes are supported for validation, routes, etc.
Symfony's AssetMapper serves and versions CSS/JS using importmap.php without needing Node.js or webpack.
Symfony 6.4 is an LTS (long-term support) release with bug fixes until November 2027 and security fixes until November 2028.
Major Symfony releases (e.g., 6.0) remove the deprecations from the previous branch (5.x); deprecations only trigger within a minor series.
Every Symfony major release includes an UPGRADE guide documenting the changes.
The Symfony AssetMapper component serves and versioned-manages assets and handles importmaps without needing Node.js or Webpack.
Symfony 8.2 is scheduled for release at the end of November 2026, so it has not been released as of 2026-11-07.
Symfony follows a predictable six-month release cycle, so after 8.0 (Nov 2025) and 8.1 (May 2026), 8.2 is scheduled for November 2026.
Symfony uses standard minor version increments, so the version following 8.1 is 8.2.
Symfony 8.2 doesn't exist, and Symfony minor releases never require rewriting applications—they maintain backward compatibility.
PHP maintains backward compatibility within a major branch, so minor version updates like 8.1 → 8.2 should work without code changes, although rare edge-case behavior adjustments can occur.
Symfony follows a pattern where the last minor release of a major branch is x.4 (LTS), so 8.4 is released just before Symfony 9.0.
Symfony 8.2 does not require PHP 8.5; Symfony 8.x supports PHP 8.3+ (8.2 is not even a current Symfony release).
Symfony's policy keeps deprecations for the entire major version, so features deprecated in 8.x are only removed in 9.0.
Twig is a sandboxed template engine that only allows registered filters, functions, and methods, not arbitrary PHP code.
Twig's default autoescape option is set to 'html', so printed variables are escaped by default.
The Twig |e filter escapes a string for safe output, defaulting to the HTML context.
The format_number filter in twig/intl-extra formats a number according to a given locale.
In Twig, the |raw filter marks a value as safe, preventing it from being auto-escaped.
In Twig, {{ }} outputs expression values and {% %} executes logic tags like if, for, and set.
Twig allows declaring variables inside templates using the {% set %} tag.
Twig's dump() function outputs the debug structure of a variable when debugging is enabled.
Bootstrap provides CSS and JavaScript UI components, while SPA frameworks like Angular, React, or Vue handle application structure.
The .container class provides a responsive fixed-width container whose max-width changes at each breakpoint.
Bootstrap's grid uses 12 columns, not 16 (though it historically did rely on floats in older versions).
In Bootstrap 5 the infixes used in class names are sm, md, lg, xl, and xxl — five of them, since the smallest tier (xs) has no infix.
In Bootstrap, spacing utilities like mt-3 use a scale where each step is a multiple of the $spacer variable (default 1rem).
Bootstrap 5 uses the data-bs-toggle attribute (e.g. data-bs-toggle="dropdown") to initialize interactive components.
Bootstrap 5 removed the jQuery dependency and all components are written in vanilla JavaScript.
Bootstrap 5.3 enables dark mode with the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute, not a .dark class.
Doctrine requires schema creation via migration or schema tool commands; it does not create tables automatically at runtime.
EntityManager::persist() schedules a new entity for management, with SQL deferred until flush().
EntityManager::merge() was deprecated in Doctrine ORM 2.x and removed in ORM 3, so it no longer exists.
Doctrine Query Language operates on entities and their properties, which Doctrine translates into SQL over tables and columns.
Doctrine's find() returns null when no entity matches the given id.
DoctrineBundle does not automatically call flush(); you must explicitly call it on the EntityManager to persist changes.
Doctrine's Unit of Work tracks managed entities, so changes are flushed without calling persist() again.
remove() (Doctrine's removal method) only marks the entity for deletion; the DELETE query is executed when flush() is called.
MVCC in PostgreSQL allows readers and writers to work concurrently without blocking each other.
EXPLAIN shows the query execution plan without running the query.
Both create an auto-incrementing integer column backed by a sequence; IDENTITY is just the SQL-standard syntax for the same mechanism.
PostgreSQL treats NULLs as distinct, so a UNIQUE constraint allows multiple rows with NULL by default.
PostgreSQL's string_agg(value, separator) aggregate concatenates strings with a delimiter.
Plain VACUUM only marks dead tuple space as reusable within the table file; only VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and returns space to the operating system.
In a window function's OVER clause, PARTITION BY splits rows into groups the function is computed over independently.
READ COMMITTED only prevents dirty reads; non-repeatable reads are still possible since each query sees the latest committed data.
PostgreSQL by default runs in autocommit mode, executing and committing each statement in its own implicit transaction unless an explicit BEGIN is issued.
The COMMIT command ends a transaction and makes all its changes permanent.
Indexes help find rows for UPDATE/DELETE WHERE clauses, just like in SELECT queries.
PostgreSQL supports SAVEPOINT to allow partial rollbacks within a transaction.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query to show real row counts and timing; plain EXPLAIN only shows the plan without running it.
pgvector is the PostgreSQL extension that provides vector data types and similarity search indexes for embeddings.
A partial index includes only the rows that satisfy the WHERE condition, making it smaller and faster for matching queries.
PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE via Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which uses predicate-based conflict detection rather than locking the rows read.
HTTP 201 means 'Created', indicating the request resulted in a new resource being created.
HTTP 204 No Content indicates success with an empty response body.
Per the HTTP specification, DELETE is idempotent—repeatedly deleting the same resource leaves the end state the same (the resource remains deleted).
Access-Control-Allow-Origin is a response header sent by the server to permit cross-origin requests from clients.
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given time, exceeding a rate limit.
It's reversed: 4xx codes indicate client errors and 5xx codes indicate server errors.
The Content-Type header specifies the MIME type of the request or response body.
RFC 5789 defines PATCH as not necessarily idempotent, while PUT is required to be idempotent.
You must use a timing-safe comparison such as password_verify() or hash_equals() to prevent timing attacks.
CSRF tokens are generated server-side, stored in the session, and checked on each unsafe request to confirm the request originated from the legitimate site.
The CSP policy is delivered via the Content-Security-Policy HTTP header.
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework, not authentication; access tokens grant access to resources and don't reliably identify the user (that's OpenID Connect's role).
XSS is prevented by escaping output in the HTML context (e.g., htmlspecialchars), not merely by validating input before storage.
The authorization server returns an authorization code to the redirect_uri, which the client exchanges for an access token.
Refresh tokens are long-lived and are used to obtain new access tokens without requiring the user to re-authenticate.
Salts are not secret—they are typically stored alongside the hash, since verification requires the same salt, and their purpose is only to prevent precomputed rainbow-table attacks.
Test methods must be defined in a class that extends PHPUnit's TestCase (or use the @Test annotation in older versions) to be discovered and run.
setUp() runs before each test method; setUpBeforeClass() runs once before all tests.
A data provider supplies multiple sets of arguments, so the test runs once per set.
The expectException() method declares that a test expects an exception of the given class to be thrown.
It's reversed: mocks verify which methods were called, while stubs only return predetermined data.
In PHPUnit 10+, metadata moved to native PHP attributes like #[DataProvider], and the @dataProvider annotation is deprecated in favor of them.
PHPUnit supports test dependencies via the @depends annotation, allowing a test to receive the result of another test.
PHPUnit supports ordering tests randomly via the --order-by=random option.
